      Ze binds the outbound udp4 socket to this address, so every Access-Request leaves with it as the source. An IPv4 address here is also sent as NAS-IP-Address (RFC 2865 Section 4.1). Where the leaf is absent, the kernel picks the address of the outgoing interface and no NAS-IP-Address is sent. NAS-Identifier carries the hostname of this device either way, so the request meets Section 4.1 with the leaf unset. An address this host does not hold refuses the bind, and Ze logs the failure. The RADIUS backend then contributes nothing, and login falls through to the local accounts.
    - **timeout** `uint16`: Per-server request timeout in seconds
      The value bounds the wait for one answer from one server. Each wait after a miss doubles the one before it. The default 3 therefore waits 3 seconds, then 6, then 12, across the three transmissions the default retries allows. The range is 1 to 60 seconds. The time one login spends on RADIUS is capped at 2 minutes, whatever timeout and retries hold. The login then falls through to the local accounts.
  - **tacacs** `container`: TACACS+ server configuration (RFC 8907)
    The TACACS+ backend joins the AAA chain at priority 100, in front of the local backend at priority 200. Ze builds the backend only where the server list holds one entry or more, so a container with no server leaves the chain unchanged. Authentication runs as soon as one server exists. The authorization leaf and the accounting leaf each turn on their own half.
    - **accounting** `boolean`: Enable command execution accounting
      Set it true and Ze sends an accounting record for each command a user runs. One background worker sends the records, so a slow server does not delay the command. The queue holds 64 records, and Ze counts each record it drops because the queue is full. That count is what shows a server which cannot keep up.
    - **authorization** `boolean`: Enable per-command TACACS+ authorization
      The default false authorizes each command from the local profiles alone and sends the server nothing. Set it true and Ze sends an AUTHOR REQUEST for each command, with service=shell, cmd=<verb> and one cmd-arg for each argument (RFC 8907 Section 6). PASS_ADD and PASS_REPL run the command, and FAIL refuses it. Ze sends privilege level 1 on every one of these requests.
    - **server <address>** `list`: TACACS+ servers, tried in configured order
      Ze tries the servers in the order you write them and moves to the next one when a connection or an exchange fails. The order is the config order, because the list is ordered-by user. Where every server fails, the AAA chain moves on to the local backend, so the local accounts still answer.
      - **key** `string`: Shared secret this server obfuscates its packets with
        The key is the shared secret RFC 8907 Section 4.5 builds the MD5 pseudo-pad from, and both ends must hold the same value. A client with no secret has no conformant packet to send. Section 10.5.2 requires a shared secret and forbids a client to set TAC_PLUS_UNENCRYPTED_FLAG. Omitting the key refuses a commit, through the AAA rebuild rather than through the schema: a missing mandatory field is only a warning. At BOOT the same failure is logged and this backend is DROPPED from the chain. A user who exists locally still logs in, and the local profiles still govern the command. The leaf is marked sensitive, so every display path prints a placeholder. A $9$-encoded value written by hand is decoded on read, and the commit path writes back what you typed.
      - **port** `uint16`: TCP port (default 49)
        Port 49 is the port IANA assigns to TACACS+, and RFC 8907 Section 3.4 names it. Ze opens one TCP connection to this port and reuses it where the server agrees to the single-connect flag. The type sets no lower bound, so a commit takes 0 and every connection to that server then fails.
    - **source-address** `ip-address`: Source IP for outbound TACACS+ connections
      Ze binds the local end of the outbound TCP connection to this address. Use it where the TACACS+ server accepts one address for this device, for example a loopback address. Where the leaf is absent, the kernel picks the address of the outgoing interface.
    - **strict-fallback** `boolean`: Deny authorization when TACACS+ is unavailable instead of falling back to local RBAC
      The leaf decides one case: the server did not answer, or it answered ERROR or a status Ze does not know. The default false then authorizes the command from the local profiles, so a server outage does not lock the operator out. Set it true and Ze refuses the command instead. Neither value changes a FAIL from the server, which always refuses the command. The leaf reaches nothing while authorization is false.
    - **timeout** `uint16`: Per-server connection timeout in seconds
      The value bounds two things for each server: the TCP connect, and the read of one exchange. Ze gives it to net.Dialer.Timeout and to the deadline of the connection. With four servers and the default 5, a full failover takes at most 20 seconds before the AAA chain reaches the local backend.
  - **tacacs-profile <level>** `list`: Maps TACACS+ privilege level to ze authorization profile
    The list turns the privilege level Ze resolves for a session into the ze authorization profiles of that session. A level with no entry here denies the login, so this mapping is what grants access, and not the PASS from the server. Ze also removes a reserved profile name from the set, and a level that then resolves to nothing denies the login too.
    - **profile** `string[]`: Ze authorization profiles for this privilege level. At least one is required.
      A level mapped to no profiles would authenticate the user and grant nothing. Authorization reads an empty profile set as 'no opinion' rather than 'deny'. To deny a privilege level, leave the level out of the mapping.
  - **user <name>** `list`: Authenticated user (local)
    Authenticated user (local). Each entry is one local account. password carries the bcrypt hash the login compares against, and profile names the authorization profiles the account carries. A commit rejects an entry whose name is reserved for a built-in identity.
    - **password** `string`: Bcrypt-hashed password, in canonical form.
      The canonical form carries a cost prefix, for example $2a$10$ before the salt and the digest. Write the plaintext password to plaintext-password. On commit, ze hashes that value into this leaf and then discards the plaintext.
    - **plaintext-password** `string`: Write-only plaintext password.
      On commit, the config system hashes this value with bcrypt into the canonical password leaf, and it removes this leaf from the tree. Ze never writes the value to the config file. A display path renders the secret placeholder in its place.
    - **profile** `string[]`: Authorization profile name(s) assigned to this user
      Authorization profile names assigned to this user. A commit rejects a name that no profile under system authorization defines, and it rejects a reserved name. Once one profile exists, a user with no name here authenticates and is then denied every command.
    - **public-keys <name>** `list`: SSH public keys for key-based authentication. Each entry is a named key (e.g. user@host).
      Ze joins the type and the key of each entry into one authorized_keys line. A client key that equals any entry of this user authenticates that user. A key that does not parse is logged and skipped, and the other keys of the user still match. A user that carries a key and no profile authenticates, and the authorizer then decides what they can run.
      - **key** `string`: Base64-encoded public key data.
        The value is the middle field of an SSH public key line. It carries no type prefix and no comment suffix.
      - **type** `enumeration`: SSH public key algorithm.
        The algorithm is the first field of an SSH public key line, such as ssh-ed25519.
        - `ecdsa-sha2-nistp256`: An ECDSA key on the NIST P-256 curve.
        - `ecdsa-sha2-nistp384`: An ECDSA key on the NIST P-384 curve.
        - `ecdsa-sha2-nistp521`: An ECDSA key on the NIST P-521 curve.
        - `ssh-ed25519`: An Ed25519 key.
        - `ssh-rsa`: An RSA key.
- **authorization** `container`: Profile-based command authorization
  Profile-based command authorization. Ze builds the authorization store only when this container holds at least one profile. With no profile written, no store exists and every authenticated user runs every command. The first profile therefore changes the answer for every user, and a user with no profile assigned is denied from that point. A backend that FAILS TO BUILD is dropped and the chain composes without it, so these profiles still govern where the local backend survived. Where every backend fails, nothing authenticates and every command is refused.
  - **profile <name>** `list`: Named authorization profile with run and edit sections
    Named authorization profile with a run section and an edit section. A user can carry several profiles. Ze takes the action of the first profile that holds a matching entry. When no entry of any profile matches, the section default of the first profile applies.
    - **edit** `container`: Configuration command authorization (write commands)
      Configuration command authorization, which is the set of commands that change the config. Ze evaluates this section for every command the dispatcher does not mark read-only.
      - **default-action** `enumeration`: Action when no entry matches
        Action when no entry of this section matches the command. Ze reads the value allow, and it leaves the section at deny for every other state, the absent leaf included. A user who carries several profiles falls back to the default of the first profile whose section was reached.
        - `allow`: Permit a command that no entry of this section matches.
        - `deny`: Refuse a command that no entry of this section matches.
      - **entry <number>** `list`: Ordered authorization entry
        Ordered authorization entry. Ze sorts the entries of the section by number and takes the action of the first one that matches. A command that matches no entry falls to default-action. An entry with an empty match is rejected at commit.
        - **action** `enumeration`: Authorization action
          Authorization action for a command this entry matches. Ze reads the value allow, and it leaves the entry at deny for every other state, the absent leaf included. The first matching entry decides, so a deny stops the search even where a later entry allows.
          - `allow`: Permit the command this entry matches and stop the search.
          - `deny`: Refuse the command this entry matches and stop the search.
        - **match** `string`: Command path prefix or regex pattern
          Command path prefix, or a regular expression when regex is true. A prefix comparison ignores case and stops at a word boundary. 'show bgp' therefore matches 'show bgp' and 'show bgp summary', and it does not match 'show bgpx'. An empty match is rejected at commit. A match that names no command Ze knows is logged as a warning and kept, because a plugin can register its commands later.
        - **regex** `boolean`: If true, match is a regular expression
          If true, match is a regular expression. Ze compiles the pattern at commit and rejects one it cannot compile. The pattern is not anchored, so it matches anywhere inside the command text. Write ^ and $ where the whole command has to match. A regex entry is case sensitive, unlike a prefix entry.
    - **run** `container`: Operational command authorization (read-only commands)
      Operational command authorization, which is the set of read-only commands. Ze evaluates this section when the dispatcher marks the command read-only, and the edit section for every other command.
      - **default-action** `enumeration`: Action when no entry matches
        Action when no entry of this section matches the command. Ze reads the value allow, and it leaves the section at deny for every other state, the absent leaf included. A user who carries several profiles falls back to the default of the first profile whose section was reached.
        - `allow`: Permit a command that no entry of this section matches.
        - `deny`: Refuse a command that no entry of this section matches.
      - **entry <number>** `list`: Ordered authorization entry
        Ordered authorization entry. Ze sorts the entries of the section by number and takes the action of the first one that matches. A command that matches no entry falls to default-action. An entry with an empty match is rejected at commit.
        - **action** `enumeration`: Authorization action
          Authorization action for a command this entry matches. Ze reads the value allow, and it leaves the entry at deny for every other state, the absent leaf included. The first matching entry decides, so a deny stops the search even where a later entry allows.
          - `allow`: Permit the command this entry matches and stop the search.
          - `deny`: Refuse the command this entry matches and stop the search.
        - **match** `string`: Command path prefix or regex pattern
          Command path prefix, or a regular expression when regex is true. A prefix comparison ignores case and stops at a word boundary. 'show bgp' therefore matches 'show bgp' and 'show bgp summary', and it does not match 'show bgpx'. An empty match is rejected at commit. A match that names no command Ze knows is logged as a warning and kept, because a plugin can register its commands later.
        - **regex** `boolean`: If true, match is a regular expression
          If true, match is a regular expression. Ze compiles the pattern at commit and rejects one it cannot compile. The pattern is not anchored, so it matches anywhere inside the command text. Write ^ and $ where the whole command has to match. A regex entry is case sensitive, unlike a prefix entry.
- **commit-revisions** `uint16`: Maximum number of config archive files kept per file:// location.
  After each archive write, Ze prunes the files beyond this count, oldest first. 0 disables the pruning and keeps every file. The count applies to a file:// archive only, and Ze never prunes an HTTP archive.
- **conntrack** `container`: Connection tracking (conntrack) module loading, table tuning, and timeout configuration.
  The container holds the helper modules to load, the table bounds, the protocol timeouts and the TCP behavior flags. Ze writes each one to its net.netfilter sysctl key.
  - **accounting** `empty`: Enable per-connection byte/packet counters (nf_conntrack_acct).
    Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_acct. The counters cost memory per flow, so the kernel keeps them off until they are asked for.
  - **checksum** `empty`: Enable conntrack checksum verification (nf_conntrack_checksum).
    Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_checksum. The kernel then drops a packet whose checksum is wrong before it tracks the flow.
  - **expect-max** `uint16`: Maximum expected connections (nf_conntrack_expect_max).
    Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_expect_max. An expectation is the second flow a helper predicts, such as an FTP data connection.
  - **hash-size** `uint32`: Conntrack hash table buckets (nf_conntrack_buckets).
    Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_buckets. More buckets shorten each hash chain, and cost more memory.
  - **log-invalid** `enumeration`: Log invalid packets for the specified protocol (nf_conntrack_log_invalid).
    Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_log_invalid. The values are all, tcp, udp, icmp and icmpv6.
    - `all`: Log all invalid packets.
    - `icmp`: Log invalid ICMP packets.
    - `icmpv6`: Log invalid ICMPv6 packets.
    - `tcp`: Log invalid TCP packets.
    - `udp`: Log invalid UDP packets.
  - **module** `enumeration[]`: Conntrack helper modules to load.
    The leaf-list only loads a module. Removing a module from the list stops the load on the next boot, and it does not unload the module at runtime.
    - `amanda`: Amanda helper (nf_conntrack_amanda).
    - `ftp`: FTP helper (nf_conntrack_ftp).
    - `h323`: H.323 helper (nf_conntrack_h323).
    - `irc`: IRC helper (nf_conntrack_irc).
    - `netbios-ns`: NetBIOS-NS helper (nf_conntrack_netbios_ns).
    - `nfs`: NFS helper (nf_conntrack_nfs).
    - `pptp`: PPTP helper (nf_conntrack_pptp).
    - `sane`: SANE helper (nf_conntrack_sane).
    - `sip`: SIP helper (nf_conntrack_sip). May break VoIP NAT traversal.
    - `snmp`: SNMP helper (nf_conntrack_snmp).
    - `sqlnet`: SQLnet/TNS helper (nf_conntrack_sqlnet).
    - `tftp`: TFTP helper (nf_conntrack_tftp).
  - **table-size** `uint32`: Maximum conntrack table entries (nf_conntrack_max).
    Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max. The table holds no more flows than this, and a new flow past the bound is dropped.
  - **tcp** `container`: TCP connection tracking behavior flags.
    The container holds the four TCP flags, and Ze writes each one to its net.netfilter key.
    - **be-liberal** `boolean`: Accept out-of-window packets for established connections.
      Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal. With true the kernel tracks a packet outside the window rather than marking it INVALID.
    - **ignore-invalid-rst** `boolean`: Ignore RST packets with invalid sequence numbers.
      Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_ignore_invalid_rst. With true the kernel drops such a RST rather than closing the flow on it.
    - **loose** `boolean`: Allow tracking connections started before conntrack loaded.
      Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_loose. With true the kernel picks up a flow whose handshake it never saw.
    - **max-retrans** `uint8`: Maximum retransmissions before marking connection invalid.
      Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_max_retrans. The kernel marks the flow INVALID past this many retransmissions.
  - **timeout** `container`: Connection tracking timeouts per protocol.
    The container holds one sub-container per protocol. Ze writes each leaf to its own net.netfilter timeout key.
    - **dccp** `container`: DCCP connection tracking timeouts.
      The container holds one leaf per DCCP state, and Ze writes each one to its net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_dccp_timeout_* key.
      - **closereq** `uint32`: Close-request timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_dccp_timeout_closereq. It bounds a connection the server is closing.
      - **closing** `uint32`: Closing timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_dccp_timeout_closing. It bounds a connection that is closing.
      - **open** `uint32`: Open timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_dccp_timeout_open. An idle open connection leaves the table after this many seconds.
      - **partopen** `uint32`: Partopen timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_dccp_timeout_partopen. It bounds a connection that is half open.
      - **request** `uint32`: Request timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_dccp_timeout_request. It bounds a connection whose request got no answer.
      - **respond** `uint32`: Respond timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_dccp_timeout_respond. It bounds a connection that answered the request.
      - **timewait** `uint32`: Time-wait timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_dccp_timeout_timewait. It bounds a closed connection the kernel holds against a late packet.
    - **generic** `uint32`: Generic timeout in seconds (nf_conntrack_generic_timeout).
      Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_generic_timeout. The kernel uses it for a protocol that has no timeout of its own.
    - **gre** `container`: GRE connection tracking timeouts.
      The container holds the two GRE timeouts, and Ze writes each one to its net.netfilter key.
      - **stream** `uint32`: Stream timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_gre_timeout_stream. It bounds a GRE flow that has seen traffic in both directions.
      - **timeout** `uint32`: Default timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_gre_timeout. It bounds a GRE flow that has seen traffic in one direction.
    - **icmp** `container`: ICMP connection tracking timeouts.
      The container holds the ICMP timeout, and Ze writes it to its net.netfilter key.
      - **timeout** `uint32`: Timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_icmp_timeout. It bounds an ICMP flow, such as an echo request that waits for its reply.
    - **icmpv6** `container`: ICMPv6 connection tracking timeouts.
      The container holds the ICMPv6 timeout, and Ze writes it to its net.netfilter key.
      - **timeout** `uint32`: Timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_icmpv6_timeout. It bounds an ICMPv6 flow, such as an echo request that waits for its reply.
    - **sctp** `container`: SCTP connection tracking timeouts.
      The container holds one leaf per SCTP state, and Ze writes each one to its net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_sctp_timeout_* key.
      - **closed** `uint32`: Closed timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_sctp_timeout_closed. It bounds an association in the CLOSED state.
      - **cookie-echoed** `uint32`: Cookie-echoed timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_sc tp_timeout_cookie_echoed. It bounds an association that echoed the cookie.
      - **cookie-wait** `uint32`: Cookie-wait timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_sctp_timeout_cookie_wait. It bounds an association that waits for the cookie.
      - **established** `uint32`: Established timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_sctp_timeout_established. An idle established association leaves the table after this many seconds.
      - **heartbeat-sent** `uint32`: Heartbeat-sent timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_sc tp_timeout_heartbeat_sent. It bounds an association that waits for the heartbeat answer.
      - **shutdown-ack-sent** `uint32`: Shutdown-ACK-sent timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_sc tp_timeout_shutdown_ack_sent. It bounds an association that waits for the shutdown ACK.
      - **shutdown-recd** `uint32`: Shutdown-received timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_sc tp_timeout_shutdown_recd. It bounds an association the far end is closing.
      - **shutdown-sent** `uint32`: Shutdown-sent timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_sc tp_timeout_shutdown_sent. It bounds an association this end is closing.
    - **tcp** `container`: TCP connection tracking timeouts.
      The container holds one leaf per TCP state, and Ze writes each one to its net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_* key.
      - **close** `uint32`: Close timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_close. It bounds a flow that a RST closed.
      - **close-wait** `uint32`: Close-wait timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_close_wait. It bounds a flow the far end has closed.
      - **established** `uint32`: Established timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established. An idle established flow leaves the table after this many seconds.
      - **fin-wait** `uint32`: FIN-wait timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_fin_wait. It bounds a flow this end has closed.
      - **last-ack** `uint32`: Last-ACK timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_last_ack. It bounds a flow that waits for the last ACK.
      - **max-retrans** `uint32`: Max retransmission timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_max_retrans. It bounds a flow that passed the retransmission limit.
      - **syn-recv** `uint32`: SYN-received timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_syn_recv. It bounds a half-open flow that got a SYN and no final ACK.
      - **syn-sent** `uint32`: SYN-sent timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_syn_sent. It bounds a flow whose SYN got no answer.
      - **time-wait** `uint32`: Time-wait timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_time_wait. It bounds a closed flow the kernel holds against a late packet.
      - **unacknowledged** `uint32`: Unacknowledged timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tc p_timeout_unacknowledged. It bounds a flow whose data no ACK covers.
    - **udp** `container`: UDP connection tracking timeouts.
      The container holds the two UDP timeouts, and Ze writes each one to its net.netfilter key.
      - **stream** `uint32`: Stream timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_udp_timeout_stream. It bounds a UDP flow that has seen traffic in both directions.
      - **timeout** `uint32`: Default timeout (seconds).
        Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_udp_timeout. It bounds a UDP flow that has seen traffic in one direction.
  - **timestamp** `empty`: Enable per-connection timestamps (nf_conntrack_timestamp).
    Ze writes the value to net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_timestamp. The kernel then records the start time of each flow.
- **console** `container`: Serial console configuration for headless CPE devices.
  The container holds the serial devices Ze runs a console on. A headless device has no other way in when the network is down.
  - **device <name>** `list`: Serial device to configure as console.
    Each entry names one serial device, and it carries the baud rate of that device.
    - **speed** `enumeration`: Baud rate (default 115200).
      The rates are 9600, 19200, 38400, 57600 and 115200 baud. The default is 115200.
      - `115200`: 115200 baud.
      - `19200`: 19200 baud.
      - `38400`: 38400 baud.
      - `57600`: 57600 baud.
      - `9600`: 9600 baud.
- **crash-dump** `container`: Kernel crash capture, kept across a reboot and listed by show crashes.
  A Go panic is already captured. This container covers the kernel panic, which leaves no process behind to write a report. The kernel writes its own record into a reserved memory region, and Ze reads it on the next boot. The reservation is a kernel boot argument, so it is armed by the next boot of an image built with image.crash-dump, not by the commit.
  - **enabled** `boolean`: Store the kernel panic record as a crash report at the next boot.
    Ze reads the record the kernel left, writes it into the crash directory as a kernel-kind report, and clears the region so the next fault has room. Run 'show crashes' to read whether the running kernel is armed as well as configured.
  - **memory-image** `container`: Full memory image capture, for a fault a backtrace does not explain.
    A backtrace names the faulting subsystem, which is what a bug report needs. A memory image is sized to RAM and costs the write time while the router is down, so it is off by default and reported as unarmed until the target has room for it.
    - **enabled** `boolean`: Capture a full memory image as well as the panic backtrace.
      Refused on a build that cannot stage a capture kernel, which today means anything other than amd64. Reported as configured but not armed when the crash directory has less free space than the image needs, with the shortfall in bytes.
    - **reserve** `uint16`: Memory reserved for the capture kernel that writes the image.
      The capture kernel runs after the fault and needs its own memory, separate from the region holding the backtrace. The range is 64 to 1024 megabytes. It is a floor on the space estimate: the image itself is sized to RAM.
  - **reserve** `uint16`: Memory the kernel reserves to write its panic record into.
    The region is taken from RAM on every boot, so it is sized for a backtrace rather than for a memory image. The range is 4 to 256 megabytes and the default of 16 holds a full backtrace. The appliance build renders the size onto the kernel command line, so a change takes effect at the next image build.
- **dns** `container`: DNS resolver tuning and resolv.conf settings.
  The container holds the resolv.conf path, the query timeout, the cache bounds and the DNSSEC validation mode.
  - **cache-size** `uint32`: Maximum cached entries (0 disables caching).
    The cache holds this many answers at most, and 0 disables it. The range is 0 to 1000000, and the default is 10000.
  - **cache-ttl** `uint32`: Maximum cache TTL in seconds (0 uses response TTL only).
    Ze holds an answer for the TTL the response carries, and never longer than this value. 0 keeps the response TTL alone. The default is 86400 seconds.
  - **dnssec-validation** `enumeration`: Upstream-answer DNSSEC validation for the stub resolver.
    RFC 4035 defines the stub model. off leaves resolution unchanged. permissive and strict set the EDNS0 DO bit, and rely on a validating upstream (CD=0) to answer SERVFAIL on a broken chain. strict rejects such an answer as an error. permissive logs it and returns the empty result. An insecure zone and an unsigned zone (NOERROR, AD=0) are always accepted.
    - `off`: No DNSSEC handling, and no DO bit. This is the default.
    - `permissive`: Request DNSSEC, and log a broken chain without failing.
    - `strict`: Request DNSSEC, and reject an answer on a broken chain.
  - **resolv-conf-path** `string`: Path Ze writes the DNS servers to, as a resolv.conf file.
    The default /tmp/resolv.conf suits gokrazy, whose rootfs is read-only. Set /etc/resolv.conf on standard Linux. An empty string stops Ze writing the file.
  - **timeout** `uint16`: Query timeout in seconds.
    Ze waits this long for an answer before it gives up on a query. The range is 1 to 60 seconds, and the default is 5.
- **domain** `string`: System domain, supports $ENV_VAR expansion.
  Ze expands a $ENV_VAR reference in the value when it reads the config.
- **host** `string`: System hostname, supports $ENV_VAR expansion.
  Ze expands a $ENV_VAR reference in the value when it reads the config.
- **name-server** `ip-address[]`: Static DNS name servers, written to resolv.conf and used by ze internal resolver.
  Ze writes each address to the resolv.conf file named by dns/resolv-conf-path, and its own resolver asks these servers.
- **peeringdb** `container`: PeeringDB API configuration for prefix data lookups.
  The container holds the API base URL and the prefix-limit margin. Ze asks PeeringDB for the prefix counts of a peer.
  - **margin** `uint8`: Percentage margin above PeeringDB count for prefix maximum (0-100).
    Ze multiplies the PeeringDB prefix count by this margin, in percent, and uses the result as the prefix limit. The range is 0 to 100, and the default is 10.
  - **url** `string`: PeeringDB-compatible API base URL.
    Ze sends each query to this base URL. The default is https://www.peeringdb.com. Set another URL to reach a mirror or a test server.
- **rir** `container`: Regional Internet Registry delegation table settings.
  The container holds one delegation-source block per registry. `update resolve rir` reads the delegation file of every registry, and a block names where one of the five is read from.
  - **delegation-source <registry>** `list`: Per-registry source of the delegation file.
    One block names one registry and the URL its delegation file is read from. A registry with no block is read from the file that registry publishes, so mirroring one registry takes one block.
    - **url** `string`: URL Ze reads this registry's delegation file from.
      Ze reads the file with one GET, and the URL carries the scheme, the host and the path of that one file. A mirror publishes five files, so it takes five blocks.
- **tuning** `container`: Runtime hardware tuning applied at startup and on config commit.
  The container holds the CPU governor, the IRQ affinity list and the ethtool settings. The tuning runs on Linux, and it needs root or CAP_SYS_ADMIN.
  - **cpu** `container`: CPU frequency scaling tuning.
    The container holds the scaling governor Ze writes to each core.
    - **governor** `enumeration`: CPU scaling governor applied to all cores.
      Ze writes the governor to every core. The values are performance, powersave, ondemand, conservative and schedutil.
      - `conservative`: Gradual frequency scaling.
      - `ondemand`: Dynamic frequency scaling.
      - `performance`: Maximum frequency.
      - `powersave`: Minimum frequency.
      - `schedutil`: Scheduler-driven frequency scaling.
  - **ethtool <interface>** `list`: Per-interface ethtool settings.
    Each entry names one interface and holds the ethtool settings Ze applies to it.
    - **ring** `container`: Ring buffer sizes.
      The container holds the receive ring size and the transmit ring size of the interface.
      - **rx** `uint16`: Receive ring buffer size.
        Ze asks the driver for a receive ring of this many descriptors. The range is 1 to 65535, and a driver refuses a size it cannot serve.
      - **tx** `uint16`: Transmit ring buffer size.
        Ze asks the driver for a transmit ring of this many descriptors. The range is 1 to 65535, and a driver refuses a size it cannot serve.
  - **irq-affinity <interface>** `list`: Pin NIC IRQs to specific CPUs.
    Each entry names one interface, and Ze pins the IRQs of that interface to the CPUs the entry lists.
    - **cpus** `string`: CPU list, for example 0,2,4-7.
      The list takes a single CPU, a comma-separated set, and a range with a hyphen.
- **update-check** `container`: System version check and platform update settings.
  On gokrazy, gokrazy manages the image updates.
  - **auto-apply** `boolean`: Download, verify, and stage a Ze binary update without an operator.
    With true, Ze downloads, verifies and stages a binary update on a platform Ze manages. With false, Ze only checks the version and reports it.
  - **interval** `uint32`: Check interval in seconds (default 86400 = daily, minimum 60).
    Ze checks the version once in this interval. The range is 60 to 604800 seconds, and the default is 86400, which is one day.
  - **maintenance-window** `container`: Time window when binary replacement may occur. Download and verification proceed at any time.
    Ze reads the window only when start and end both carry a time. Ze downloads and verifies at any hour, and it waits for the window before it replaces the binary. Outside the window Ze reports that the update waits, and it keeps the verified file.
    - **end** `string`: End time HH:MM in local time.
      The end is not part of the window: Ze stages at start and at every minute up to end, and not at end itself. Ze refuses a value that is not HH:MM.
    - **start** `string`: Start time HH:MM in local time.
      Ze refuses a value that is not HH:MM, with an hour of 0 to 23 and a minute of 0 to 59. A start later than end makes the window cross midnight, so 22:00 to 02:00 is four hours.
  - **restart** `container`: What Ze does after it stages an update.
    An absent container leaves the restart to the operator. The container with immediate restarts after a short drain. The container with time restarts at that time each day.
    - **immediate** `empty`: Restart automatically after staging (5s drain delay). Mutually exclusive with time.
      The leaf is empty, so writing it is the whole instruction. Ze waits 5 seconds after it stages the binary and then runs the new one. Ze refuses a configuration that carries both immediate and time.
    - **time** `string`: Daily restart time, HH:MM in local time. Mutually exclusive with immediate.
      Ze stages the binary as soon as the maintenance window permits, then waits for this time of day to run it. A time outside the maintenance window is permitted, and Ze logs a warning that names both. Ze refuses a configuration that carries both immediate and time.
  - **spread** `uint32`: Maximum random delay in seconds before the download starts.
    Ze waits for the delay after it detects a new version, so that many routers do not download at the same second. 0 disables the spread.
  - **url** `string`: HTTPS URL that serves a JSON object with a 'version' field.
    One answer is {"version":"26.05.17"}. Ze compares that value against its own release version, in lexicographic order.

## telemetry

Telemetry export configuration.

The container holds the Prometheus export settings and the Netdata- compatible collector settings.

- **prometheus** `container`: Prometheus metrics HTTP export.
  The container holds the enable switch, the listen endpoints, the metrics path, the HTTP Basic Authentication settings and the collector settings.
  - **basic-auth** `container`: HTTP Basic Authentication for the Prometheus service.
    The container holds the enable switch, the realm, the username and the two password leaves.
    - **enabled** `boolean`: Require HTTP Basic Authentication on the metrics and health endpoints.
      Ze asks for no credentials while this leaf is false, and false is the default.
    - **password** `string`: Bcrypt-hashed HTTP Basic Authentication password. Write plaintext via plaintext-password.
      Ze compares the password of each request with this hash, and it compares the username in constant time. A value that is not a bcrypt hash stops the metrics server with an error, and the config check warns about it at commit. With basic-auth enabled, a username and this password are both required.
    - **plaintext-password** `string`: Write-only password.
      On commit, the config system hashes this value into password and removes this leaf. The value is never written to the config file, and a display path renders the secret placeholder for it.
    - **realm** `string`: HTTP Basic Authentication realm.
      A client shows the realm to the user when it asks for the credentials. The default is 'ze prometheus'.
    - **username** `string`: HTTP Basic Authentication username.
      The username pairs with the password leaf beside it.
  - **collector <name>** `list`: Deprecated: use netdata/collector. Per-Netdata-collector overrides (enable/disable, interval).
    Write netdata/collector instead. Ze reads this list only when the netdata container carries no collector list, and it then logs the deprecated path it read. A netdata collector list replaces this one whole, and the two are never merged.
    - **enabled** `boolean`: Enable or disable this collector.
      With false, Ze runs every other collector and stops this one. The default is true.
    - **interval** `uint16`: Override sampling interval for this collector (seconds). Inherits global interval if not set.
      The range is 1 to 60 seconds. An absent leaf gives the collector the interval of the netdata container. The leaf lives under a deprecated list, so write netdata/collector/interval instead.
  - **enabled** `boolean`: Enable the Prometheus metrics endpoint.
    Ze serves no metrics endpoint while this leaf is false, and false is the default.
  - **interval** `uint16`: Deprecated: use netdata/interval. Netdata-compatible OS collector sampling interval in seconds.
    Write netdata/interval instead. Ze reads this leaf only when the netdata container carries no interval leaf, and it then logs the deprecated path it read. The range is 1 to 60 seconds and the default is 1.
  - **netdata** `container`: Netdata-compatible OS collector metrics. These settings do not affect Ze-native metrics.
    The default of enabled is true, so an absent container still runs the collectors. The three settings under it replace the deprecated prefix, interval and collector leaves beside this container. Ze reads a deprecated leaf only when the matching leaf here is absent, and it logs the path it read.
    - **collector <name>** `list`: Per-Netdata-collector overrides of the enable state and the interval.
      Each entry names one collector, and it overrides the settings of that collector alone.
      - **enabled** `boolean`: Enable or disable this Netdata-compatible OS collector.
        With false, Ze runs every other collector and stops this one. The default is true.
      - **interval** `uint16`: Override the sampling interval of this collector, in seconds.
        When this leaf is not set, the collector uses the global Netdata interval.
    - **enabled** `boolean`: Enable the Netdata-compatible OS collectors.
      With false, Ze exports the Ze-native metrics alone. The default is true.
    - **interval** `uint16`: Netdata-compatible OS collector sampling interval in seconds.
      Each Netdata-compatible OS collector samples the operating system once in this interval. The range is 1 to 60 seconds, and the default is 1.
    - **prefix** `string`: Metric name prefix for Netdata-compatible OS collector metrics only.
      Ze puts the prefix in front of each Netdata-compatible OS collector metric name. It does not change a Ze-native metric name. The default is netdata.
  - **path** `string`: HTTP path of the metrics endpoint.
    A scraper reads the metrics at this path on each listen endpoint. The default path is /metrics.
  - **prefix** `string`: Deprecated: use netdata/prefix.
    The leaf sets the metric name prefix for Netdata-compatible OS collector metrics only.
  - **server <name>** `list`: Prometheus listen endpoints.
    Each entry names one listen endpoint. The default endpoint is 127.0.0.1 on port 9273.
    - **ip** `ip-address`: Listen IP address
      The listener binds this address. 0.0.0.0 binds every IPv4 address of the host, and :: binds every IPv6 address. Config validation refuses two listeners that share a protocol and a port when their addresses overlap. A wildcard address overlaps every address of its own family, and an IPv4 address never overlaps an IPv6 address.
    - **port** `listener-port`: Listen TCP port; 0 means OS-assigned
      The port range is 0 to 65535. Port 0 makes the operating system pick a free port at bind time, so no client can know the port before the listener starts. ze doctor tries to bind each configured endpoint and reports the one the host refuses.

## traffic

Traffic subsystem: QoS control and byte-usage accounting.

Two subtrees sit under it, and they are independent. control programs the queueing disciplines of each interface, which decides which packet leaves first. usage counts bytes with an eBPF program, and it changes no packet. Each subtree comes from its own plugin, so removing one plugin removes that subtree alone.

- **control** `container`: Traffic control configuration of each interface.
  *Provided by `traffic` ([ze-traffic-control-conf.yang](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/blob/main/internal/component/traffic/yang/ze-traffic-control-conf.yang))*
  One entry exists for each interface Ze programs. The backend leaf names the program that applies the entries.
  - **backend** `string`: Traffic control backend that programs the queueing disciplines.
    The default backend is tc, the queueing disciplines of Linux iproute2. Another backend declares itself through traffic.RegisterBackend. The ze:backend YANG extension on a feature node declares which backend supports that feature. The commit-time gate reads that extension and rejects a config that names a qdisc or a filter type the backend does not support.
  - **interface <name>** `list`: Traffic control of one named interface.
    The list key is the interface name.
    - **qdisc** `container`: The root queueing discipline of the interface.
      Ze attaches this qdisc at the root of the interface, and every class hangs beneath it.
      - **class <name>** `list`: One traffic class of the queueing discipline.
        The list key is the class name. A class carries a rate, a ceil, a priority, and the filters that select its traffic.
        - **ceil** `rate-bps`: Largest rate this class can reach.
          An absent leaf takes the value of the rate leaf.
        - **match <type>** `list`: A filter that classifies a packet into this class.
          The list key is the match type, so one class carries at most one match of each type.
          - **value** `string`: Value the filter matches.
            A mark filter takes a hex value. A dscp filter takes a DSCP name. A protocol filter takes a protocol name.
        - **priority** `uint8`: Scheduling priority of this class.
          The value 0 is the highest priority.
        - **rate** `rate-bps`: Rate this class is guaranteed.
          The value is a number and a unit, for example 10mbit or 100kbps.
      - **default-class** `string`: Name of the class that takes the unclassified traffic.
        The value is the name of a class in the class list of this qdisc.
      - **type** `qdisc-type`: Type of the queueing discipline.
        The commit-time gate rejects a type the configured backend does not support.
        - `fq`: The Fair Queue qdisc.
        - `fq_codel`: The Fair Queue Controlled Delay qdisc.
        - `hfsc`: The Hierarchical Fair Service Curve qdisc.
        - `htb`: The Hierarchical Token Bucket qdisc.
        - `netem`: The Network Emulator qdisc.
        - `prio`: The Priority qdisc.
        - `sfq`: The Stochastic Fair Queue qdisc.
        - `tbf`: The Token Bucket Filter qdisc.
- **usage** `container`: Per-interface eBPF TCX byte accounting (port/protocol always; per-IP via track-ip).
  *Provided by `traffic-usage` ([ze-traffic-usage-cmd.yang](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/blob/main/internal/plugins/trafficusage/yang/ze-traffic-usage-cmd.yang), [ze-traffic-usage-conf.yang](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/blob/main/internal/plugins/trafficusage/yang/ze-traffic-usage-conf.yang))*
  Ze attaches two eBPF programs to each accounted interface with TCX, one on ingress and one on egress. They count bytes into per-interface LRU hash maps, keyed by L4 port and protocol. Where track-ip is true they also key by IPv4 address. One poll loop reads the maps and publishes the counts as metric series. The programs count only: they drop no packet and they change none.
  - **enabled** `boolean`: Enable traffic-usage accounting.
    The default false attaches nothing and starts no poll loop. Set it true and the config also needs one enabled interface or more under interfaces. Without one, the commit is refused and the error names the missing interface list. An accounting that would report nothing never reaches the kernel.
  - **interfaces** `container`: Interfaces to account on.
    Ze accounts on the interfaces listed here and on no other. An interface with no entry is not accounted, and an entry whose enabled leaf is false is dropped before the attach. With usage enabled and this list empty, the commit is refused.
    - **interface <name>** `list`: Per-interface traffic-usage accounting.
      The entry names one interface and can override three leaves of the usage container: track-ip, stale-timeout and max-entries. What the entry does not set, it takes from the leaf of the same name under usage. An entry with a name and no body is accounted with every global value. A change to track-ip or to max-entries makes Ze detach the eBPF programs and attach them again, because both decide the shape of the maps.
      - **enabled** `boolean`: Account traffic on this interface.
        The default true accounts on the interface, so an entry with no body needs nothing more. Set it false and Ze drops the entry before it attaches anything. The accounting on that interface stops, and the rest of the list is not touched. To stop the whole feature, use the enabled leaf under usage.
      - **max-entries** `uint32`: Override the global max-entries (per-map LRU capacity) for this interface (inherits when unset).
        The leaf overrides the max-entries leaf under usage for this interface alone, and an unset leaf takes the global value. The value is the capacity of each LRU map of the interface, so it also sets the memory the interface costs. An effective value of 0 is refused at commit. A change makes Ze attach the eBPF programs again, because a map takes its capacity at creation.
      - **stale-timeout** `uint32`: Override the global stale-timeout for this interface, in milliseconds.
        0 disables the cleanup for this interface. When the leaf is unset, this interface inherits the global stale-timeout.
      - **track-ip** `boolean`: Override the global track-ip for this interface (inherits the global value when unset).
        The leaf overrides the track-ip leaf under usage for this interface alone, and an unset leaf takes the global value. True adds two more LRU maps to this interface, one for ingress and one for egress, keyed by IPv4 address. A change makes Ze attach the eBPF programs again, because the map set changes.
  - **interval** `uint32`: Map poll interval in milliseconds (100ms..1h).
    One poll loop reads every map of every accounted interface at this period, so the value sets how fresh a metric series is. The default 1000 reads once a second. A value outside 100 milliseconds to 1 hour is refused at commit. The eBPF programs count at line rate whatever this value is, so a longer interval loses no bytes.
  - **max-entries** `uint32`: Per-map LRU capacity; least-recently-used entries are evicted beyond this, keeping top talkers.
    The value is the capacity of each LRU map, and an interface takes it unless its own max-entries leaf overrides it. Ze creates two maps for each accounted interface, and two more where track-ip is true, so the value sets the memory the accounting costs. Beyond the capacity the kernel evicts the least recently used entry, which keeps the top talkers and loses the quiet ones.
  - **stale-timeout** `uint32`: Remove a metric series unseen within this many milliseconds; 0 disables cleanup.
    Ze removes a metric series it has not seen within this time, which stops the series of a talker that left from staying forever. The value 0 disables the cleanup, so every series stays until the plugin stops. An interface can override the value with its own stale-timeout leaf. An interface value that is not 0 and less than 1 second is refused at commit.
  - **track-ip** `boolean`: Account bytes per IPv4 address as well as per interface.
    The address is the source address on ingress and the destination address on egress. The default is false, which limits the number of metric series.

## vpn

*Provided by `ipsec-xfrm`*

VPN subsystems.

Ze declares one subsystem under it today, which is ipsec. That subsystem holds the ESP groups, the IKE groups and the site-to-site peers.

- **ipsec** `container`: IPsec VPN configuration.
  Ze speaks IKEv2 (RFC 7296) and installs each negotiated Child SA into the Linux XFRM stack. A peer references one ESP group and one IKE group, and those two carry the algorithms and the timers of the tunnel.
  - **cookie-threshold** `uint32`: Number of half-open IKE SAs tolerated before a COOKIE challenge.
    Number of half-open IKE SAs tolerated before an inbound IKE_SA_INIT must answer a COOKIE challenge. RFC 7296 Section 2.6 makes the challenge the answer to state and CPU exhaustion from forged source addresses. The default of 0 challenges every inbound initiation, which costs one extra round trip and stops a single spoofed datagram taking a peer's only half-open handshake slot. Raise it to tolerate that many half-open handshakes before challenging.
  - **esp-group <name>** `list`: ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) group.
    The group carries the ESP proposals a peer offers for its Child SAs and the lifetime those SAs run under. A group MUST hold at least one proposal, and commit refuses an empty one. One group holds at most 255 proposals.
    - **lifetime** `uint32`: SA lifetime in seconds. 0 disables expiry.
      The Child SA rekey trigger sits ahead of the lifetime by the larger of a random 10 percent and one retransmit budget. That lead is capped at half the lifetime. RFC 7296 Section 2.8 states the rule. 'When the lifetime of a Security Association expires, the Security Association MUST NOT be used.' Ze therefore tears the SA down at that point, even when a rekey is still in flight. The value 0 starts no rekey and no expiry.
    - **pfs** `enumeration`: Perfect Forward Secrecy for Child SA rekeying.
      With enable, Ze puts a KEi payload in the CREATE_CHILD_SA request, and the replacement Child SA is keyed from a fresh Diffie-Hellman secret. With disable, Ze sends no KEi, and the replacement is keyed from SK_d alone, so one leaked SK_d reads every replacement Child SA. RFC 7296 Section 2.17 gives both KEYMAT forms. An ESP proposal carries no Diffie-Hellman group of its own, so Ze offers the group the IKE SA already negotiated. The default is enable, and Ze refuses a response that disagrees with what its request carried.
      - `disable`: Send no KEi and key each replacement Child SA from SK_d alone.
      - `enable`: Send a KEi payload and key each replacement Child SA from a fresh Diffie-Hellman secret.
    - **proposal <number>** `list`: ESP proposal, where a lower number is a higher priority.
      ESP proposal. Lower number = higher priority. One group offers at most 255 proposals, because RFC 7296 Section 3.3.1 numbers them in one octet.
      - **encryption** `encryption-algo`: Encryption algorithm.
        No build carries a transform for chacha20poly1305 or 3des, so a proposal that names one is refused at commit. The refusal lists the algorithms the build does implement.
        - `3des`: Triple-DES-CBC (RFC 2451), deprecated. No build implements it.
        - `aes128`: AES-CBC-128 (RFC 3602).
        - `aes128ccm12`: AES-CCM-128, 12-byte ICV (RFC 4309, RFC 5282). IKE SA only.
        - `aes128ccm16`: AES-CCM-128, 16-byte ICV (RFC 4309, RFC 5282). IKE SA only.
        - `aes128ccm8`: AES-CCM-128, 8-byte ICV (RFC 4309, RFC 5282). IKE SA only.
        - `aes128gcm`: AES-GCM-128, 16-byte ICV (RFC 4106).
        - `aes256`: AES-CBC-256 (RFC 3602).
        - `aes256ccm12`: AES-CCM-256, 12-byte ICV (RFC 4309, RFC 5282). IKE SA only.
        - `aes256ccm16`: AES-CCM-256, 16-byte ICV (RFC 4309, RFC 5282). IKE SA only.
        - `aes256ccm8`: AES-CCM-256, 8-byte ICV (RFC 4309, RFC 5282). IKE SA only.
        - `aes256gcm`: AES-GCM-256, 16-byte ICV (RFC 4106).
        - `chacha20poly1305`: ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD (RFC 7634). No build implements it.
      - **hash** `hash-algo`: Integrity algorithm.
        Integrity algorithm. It is required beside a non-AEAD cipher, and refused beside an AEAD cipher. RFC 7296 Section 3.3 gives an AEAD cipher its own integrity, so an ESP proposal offers the integrity transform NONE. An ESP proposal carries no PRF transform, so this leaf never names one. No build carries a transform for sha1, so a proposal that names it is refused at commit. The refusal lists the algorithms the build does implement.
        - `sha1`: HMAC-SHA-1-96 (RFC 2404). No build implements it.
        - `sha256`: HMAC-SHA-256-128 (RFC 4868).
        - `sha384`: HMAC-SHA-384-192 (RFC 4868).
        - `sha512`: HMAC-SHA-512-256 (RFC 4868).
  - **ike-group <name>** `list`: IKE (Internet Key Exchange) group.
    The group carries the IKE proposals, the IKE SA lifetime and the Dead Peer Detection timers. A group MUST hold at least one proposal, and commit refuses an empty one. One group holds at most 255 proposals.
    - **close-action** `enumeration`: Action when peer closes the IKE SA.
      The default is none. The parser stores the value and no other code reads it, so none, start and restart leave the daemon with the same behavior. A session whose IKE SA the peer deletes tears its Child SA down and reconnects on a growing backoff. The session loop does this after every failure.
      - `none`: The default: the session reconnects on a growing backoff.
      - `restart`: Accepted and not read: the session reconnects on a growing backoff.
      - `start`: Accepted and not read: the session reconnects on a growing backoff.
    - **dead-peer-detection** `container`: Dead Peer Detection (DPD) settings (RFC 3706).
      The timers run whether or not this container is present. A peer with no DPD block probes every 30 seconds and waits 120 seconds for the answer. The probe is an empty INFORMATIONAL request, which is the liveness check of RFC 7296 Sections 1.4 and 2.4.
      - **action** `enumeration`: Action when DPD detects a dead peer.
        The default is hold. One log line reads the value when the peer is declared dead, and no other code reads it. The three values restart, hold and clear leave the same behavior. Ze deletes the Child SA, ends the session, and reconnects on a growing backoff.
        - `clear`: Log clear when the peer is dead, then reconnect on a growing backoff.
        - `hold`: Log hold when the peer is dead, then reconnect on a growing backoff.
        - `restart`: Log restart when the peer is dead, then reconnect on a growing backoff.
      - **interval** `uint16`: DPD probe interval in seconds.
        Ze sends the next probe this long after the last one, and it sends none while a probe is outstanding. The default is 30 seconds.
      - **timeout** `uint16`: DPD timeout in seconds before declaring peer dead.
        The value bounds the whole liveness budget, so it covers the first probe and every repeat of it. RFC 7296 Section 2.4 allows the verdict only when 'repeated attempts to contact it have gone unanswered for a timeout period'. Ze repeats the probe on a growing backoff inside the budget and tears the SA down when the budget runs out. The default is 120 seconds.
    - **key-exchange** `enumeration`: IKE protocol version.
      The default is ikev2 and the engine writes major version 2 into every header it sends. The parser stores the value and no other code reads it, so a group that names ikev1 commits and still runs IKEv2.
      - `ikev1`: Accepted and not read: the group still runs IKEv2.
      - `ikev2`: IKEv2 (RFC 7296), the version the engine speaks.
    - **lifetime** `uint32`: IKE SA lifetime in seconds, where 0 starts no rekey.
      Ze rekeys the IKE SA before the lifetime runs out, on the trigger the ESP group lifetime describes. It also rekeys the SA as the message id space nears its ceiling. RFC 7296 Section 2.2 requires that. 'In the unlikely event that Message IDs grow too large to fit in 32 bits, the IKE SA MUST be closed or rekeyed.' The value 0 starts no rekey, so the SA runs until the peer or the operator ends it.
    - **proposal <number>** `list`: IKE proposal, where a lower number is a higher priority.
      IKE proposal. Lower number = higher priority. One group offers at most 255 proposals, because RFC 7296 Section 3.3.1 numbers them in one octet.
      - **dh-group** `uint8`: Diffie-Hellman group number (RFC 7296 Section 3.3.2).
        The number is Transform Type 4 of RFC 7296 Section 3.3.2. That section lists the values current at publication, up to 18, and sends the reader to the IANA registry for later ones. Ze takes 1 to 31 and refuses a group this build carries no transform for. The refusal lists the numbers the build does carry, which stops the reserved Transform ID 0 reaching the wire.
      - **encryption** `encryption-algo`: Encryption algorithm.
        No build carries a transform for chacha20poly1305 or 3des, so a proposal that names one is refused at commit. The refusal lists the algorithms the build does implement.
        - `3des`: Triple-DES-CBC (RFC 2451), deprecated. No build implements it.
        - `aes128`: AES-CBC-128 (RFC 3602).
        - `aes128ccm12`: AES-CCM-128, 12-byte ICV (RFC 4309, RFC 5282). IKE SA only.
        - `aes128ccm16`: AES-CCM-128, 16-byte ICV (RFC 4309, RFC 5282). IKE SA only.
        - `aes128ccm8`: AES-CCM-128, 8-byte ICV (RFC 4309, RFC 5282). IKE SA only.
        - `aes128gcm`: AES-GCM-128, 16-byte ICV (RFC 4106).
        - `aes256`: AES-CBC-256 (RFC 3602).
        - `aes256ccm12`: AES-CCM-256, 12-byte ICV (RFC 4309, RFC 5282). IKE SA only.
        - `aes256ccm16`: AES-CCM-256, 16-byte ICV (RFC 4309, RFC 5282). IKE SA only.
        - `aes256ccm8`: AES-CCM-256, 8-byte ICV (RFC 4309, RFC 5282). IKE SA only.
        - `aes256gcm`: AES-GCM-256, 16-byte ICV (RFC 4106).
        - `chacha20poly1305`: ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD (RFC 7634). No build implements it.
      - **hash** `hash-algo`: PRF and integrity algorithm.
        It is required beside every cipher, and an AEAD cipher is no exception. RFC 7296 Section 3.3.3 makes the PRF a mandatory transform for an IKE proposal, and this leaf names it. An ESP proposal reads the same leaf as integrity alone, and refuses it beside an AEAD cipher. No build carries a transform for sha1, so a proposal that names it is refused at commit. The refusal lists the algorithms the build does implement.
        - `sha1`: HMAC-SHA-1-96 (RFC 2404). No build implements it.
        - `sha256`: HMAC-SHA-256-128 (RFC 4868).
        - `sha384`: HMAC-SHA-384-192 (RFC 4868).
        - `sha512`: HMAC-SHA-512-256 (RFC 4868).
  - **interface** `string`: WAN interface for IPsec traffic.
    Commit refuses a name no interface on the host carries. The first IPv4 address of the interface fills the local-address of every peer that names none. It is also the address the IKE socket on port 500 and the NAT-T socket on port 4500 bind to. A reload whose interface holds no IPv4 address is refused, and the same case at startup runs and writes a warning.
  - **policy <name>** `list`: Operator-authored Security Policy Database entry.
    An entry of the Security Policy Database that Ze installs directly, rather than one a Child SA negotiation produces. RFC 4301 Section 4.4.1 gives the database three dispositions: 'PROTECT, BYPASS, or DISCARD'. A peer under site-to-site produces the PROTECT entries, because those name a transform and a peer to negotiate it with. The other two name neither, so they are written here: BYPASS lets traffic cross the IPsec boundary in the clear, and DISCARD stops it at the boundary. Section 7.4 makes the discard disposition an obligation: 'All implementations MUST support DISCARDing of fragments using the normal SPD packet classification mechanisms.' This list is the management interface that Section 4.4.1 requires for it. Ze installs every entry when the configuration is applied and removes it when the entry leaves the configuration. An entry needs no peer, no key and no negotiation, so it is in force whether or not any tunnel is up.
    - **action** `enumeration`: What the entry does with the traffic its selector matches.
      RFC 4301 Section 4.4.1 defines bypass as 'to allow the packet to pass without IPsec protection' and discard as 'to discard the traffic, i.e., not to let the traffic traverse the IPsec boundary'. There is no protect here on purpose. A protect entry names an ESP transform, a mode and a peer to negotiate keys with, and those live under site-to-site peer. Offering the word in both places would put one concept in two grammars. The leaf is mandatory rather than defaulted. A defaulted disposition is the one field of this entry whose wrong value is silent: a bypass written where a discard was meant passes exactly the traffic the operator wrote the entry to stop.
      - `bypass`: Let matching traffic cross the boundary unprotected.
      - `discard`: Drop matching traffic at the boundary.
    - **direction** `enumeration`: Which side of the boundary the entry acts on.
      RFC 4301 Section 4.4.1 splits the database by direction: SPD-O holds the outbound bypass and discard entries and SPD-I holds the inbound ones. A policy is one-way, so a Ze entry is one-way too. both installs the mirrored pair: the outbound entry keeps local and remote as written, and the inbound entry swaps them, because the local side of a flow is the DESTINATION of an inbound packet. It is the default because a one-way discard leaves the return traffic crossing the boundary, which almost never expresses what the operator meant.
      - `both`: Both directions, as a mirrored pair of entries.
      - `in`: Traffic arriving from the unprotected side.
      - `out`: Traffic leaving for the unprotected side.
    - **local** `container`: The local side of the selector.
      Local is Ze's own side of the IPsec boundary. It is the source of an outbound packet and the destination of an inbound one, which is the swap direction both performs.
      - **port** `union`: Local port of the selector.
        One exact port, or any for every port. RFC 4301 Section 4.4.1.1 defines the selector as a list of ranges; the kernel selector Ze programs carries a port and a mask, which expresses every port or one exact port and no range between them. A range is refused rather than widened to any, because widening would bypass or discard traffic the operator did not name.
        - `any`: Every port.
      - **prefix** `ip-prefix`: Local traffic the entry matches.
        The value is a CIDR prefix and Ze installs it as the local selector of the policy. Use 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 for every address. The two prefixes of one entry MUST share an address family, and commit refuses a mixed pair because a kernel selector carries one family.
    - **order** `uint32`: Rank of this entry, lowest searched first.
      Where this entry sits in the operator's ordering of the Security Policy Database. A LOWER value is searched FIRST, in Ze and in the Linux kernel, and it carries the same meaning as policy-priority under a site-to-site peer. RFC 4301 Section 4.4.1: the management interface 'MUST support (total) ordering of these entries, as seen via this interface'. The default of 1000 sits between the IKE control-plane bypass at 100 and a peer's default rank of 2000, so an entry written with no order outranks the tunnels and carves its hole out of them. Raise it above 2000 to let a tunnel win instead. The range starts above 100 for the reason policy-priority states: an entry at or above the IKE bypass captures the IKE exchange that builds and rekeys every tunnel on the node.
    - **protocol** `uint8`: IP protocol number the selector matches, 0 for every protocol.
      The next-layer protocol of RFC 4301 Section 4.4.1.1, such as 6 for TCP and 17 for UDP. Zero is that section's ANY, which matches every protocol. A local-port or remote-port other than any needs this leaf to name a protocol that carries ports. Commit refuses the pair otherwise, because a port selector under protocol 0 would match on a field the classifier cannot read.
    - **remote** `container`: The remote side of the selector.
      Remote is the far side of the IPsec boundary. It is the destination of an outbound packet and the source of an inbound one.
      - **port** `union`: Remote port of the selector.
        It follows the rule the local port states: one exact port or any, and a value other than any needs the protocol leaf.
        - `any`: Every port.
      - **prefix** `ip-prefix`: Remote traffic the entry matches.
        It follows the rules the local prefix states, including the shared address family.
  - **remote-access** `container`: Remote access VPN for road warrior clients (EAP).
    The subtree parses and no session reads it, so a pool assigns no address and an eap-user authenticates nobody. The engine builds the address pool at each apply and then discards it. Configure a road warrior as a site-to-site peer with an EAP mode until the service exists. plan/immediate/spec-ipsec-remote-access.md owns the work.
    - **authentication** `container`: EAP authentication settings for remote access.
      Ze reads this block with the same parser as the site-to-site peer authentication block, so mode is mandatory here too. A handshake takes its EAP server credentials from the peer block instead, so the mode named here selects no method. The one effect it carries is the warning the daemon writes when it names eap-md5.
      - **mode** `enumeration`: EAP authentication method.
        eap-md5 establishes no shared key, and RFC 7296 Section 2.16 discourages such a method: EAP methods that do not establish a shared key SHOULD NOT be used, as they are subject to a number of man-in-the-middle attacks. The IKEv2 AUTH payloads are then keyed by SK_pi and SK_pr instead of by an EAP MSK. The method authenticates the client to Ze and tells the client nothing about Ze. The daemon writes one warning when this mode is adopted. Use eap-tls or eap-mschapv2 unless the client runs no other method.
        - `eap-md5`: EAP MD5-Challenge, Type 4 (RFC 3748 Section 5.4).
        - `eap-mschapv2`: EAP-MSCHAPv2: the client proves its password by challenge and response.
        - `eap-tls`: EAP-TLS, Type 13 (RFC 5216): the client authenticates with a certificate.
      - **x509** `container`: Server certificate references for EAP.
        Server certificate references for EAP. Ze parses both leaves and no component reads them today, so neither takes effect. Ze also leaves both unchecked, so a name that no PKI store entry carries still commits here. The enforced leaves of these names are the site-to-site peer ones.
        - **ca-certificate** `string`: Name of the CA certificate in the PKI store. It has no effect today.
          Ze compares the name against nothing, so a name no PKI store entry carries still commits. The trust anchor of a handshake comes from the ca-certificate leaf of the site-to-site peer.
        - **certificate** `string`: Name of the server certificate in the PKI store. It has no effect today.
          Ze compares the name against nothing, so a name no PKI store entry carries still commits. The certificate a handshake presents comes from the certificate leaf of the site-to-site peer.
    - **eap-user <name>** `list`: EAP user entry for remote access authentication.
      One entry holds the credential of one client. Which leaf carries that credential follows the mode of the authentication block: password for eap-mschapv2 and eap-md5, certificate for eap-tls. Ze validates every entry and no handshake reads one, because EAP runs against the credentials of the site-to-site peer.
      - **certificate** `string`: Client certificate name in PKI store. Required for eap-tls.
        Ze reads the leaf when the mode of the authentication block is eap-tls, and ignores it under every other mode. Commit refuses an empty value under eap-tls. The name is compared against nothing, so a name the PKI store does not hold still commits.
      - **password** `string`: User password ($9$-encoded). Required for eap-mschapv2.
        Ze reads the leaf when the mode of the authentication block is eap-mschapv2 or eap-md5, and ignores it under every other mode. The $9$ wrapper is removed and what is left is the password. Commit refuses an empty value under those two modes, because an empty password authenticates every client that guesses the name. The CLI writes the value back $9$-encoded and masks it in the configuration output.
    - **esp-group** `string`: Reference to an ESP group name.
      The group MUST be declared under vpn ipsec esp-group, and commit refuses a name no group carries. No other code reads the reference, because no remote access session runs.
    - **ike-group** `string`: Reference to an IKE group name.
      The group MUST be declared under vpn ipsec ike-group, and commit refuses a name no group carries. No other code reads the reference, because no remote access session runs.
    - **pool <name>** `list`: Virtual IP pool for client address assignment.
      Virtual IP pool for client address assignment (IKEv2 Configuration Payload, RFC 7296 Section 2.19).
      - **dns** `string`: DNS server pushed to clients via IKEv2 Configuration Payload.
        The leaf carries one address, and the pool sorts it into its IPv4 list or its IPv6 list from the family of that address. RFC 7296 Section 3.15.1 names the attribute that carries it INTERNAL_IP4_DNS or INTERNAL_IP6_DNS. Ze sends no Configuration payload today, so no client receives the address.
      - **domain** `string`: Search domain pushed to clients.
        The pool carries the domain beside the addresses it leases. Ze sends no Configuration payload today, so no client receives the domain.
      - **range** `string`: IPv4 CIDR for client addresses (e.g. 10.10.0.0/24). Prefix length /8-/30.
        Commit refuses a value that is not a CIDR prefix, and a prefix length outside /8 to /30. The pool leases the addresses of the prefix without the network address and the broadcast address, so a /30 carries two clients. An empty leaf leases no IPv4 address. No code reads the pool today, so no client receives an address.
      - **range6** `string`: IPv6 CIDR for client addresses (e.g. fd00::/64). Prefix length /48-/126.
        Commit refuses a value that is not a CIDR prefix, and a prefix length outside /48 to /126. An empty leaf leases no IPv6 address. No code reads the pool today, so no client receives an address.
  - **site-to-site** `container`: Site-to-site VPN peers.
    Each peer under it is one tunnel to one remote gateway. A peer carries its own algorithms, its own identity, its own traffic selectors and its own rank in the Security Policy Database.
    - **peer <name>** `list`: Remote VPN peer.
      Ze runs one session for each peer. A configuration reload stops and restarts only the peers whose own configuration changed, so a peer left untouched keeps its Child SAs up. A peer MUST reference one IKE group and one ESP group.
      - **authentication** `container`: Peer authentication settings.
        The mode leaf decides which leaf below it Ze reads. A pre-shared-secret peer and an EAP password mode read pre-shared-secret. X.509 and every EAP mode read certificate and ca-certificate, and commit refuses a peer that leaves either of those empty.
        - **ca-certificate** `string`: Name of the CA certificate in the PKI store.
          Name of the CA certificate in the PKI store. Required for every EAP mode and for X.509. It is the trust anchor the remote certificate must chain to, through any intermediate certificates the peer sends. Without it any self-signed certificate would authenticate. The remote certificate must also carry the remote-id identity in a subject alternative name. Ze reads the subject common name only when the certificate has no such extension.
        - **certificate** `string`: Name of the device certificate in the PKI store.
          Name of the device certificate in the PKI store. Required for every EAP mode, because RFC 7296 Section 2.16 makes the responder sign its AUTH with a public key. Also used by X.509 mode. Ze sends this certificate first, then the intermediate certificate the PKI entry carries.
        - **certificate-count** `uint8`: The most X.509 certificates Ze sends to this peer and accepts from it.
          The most X.509 certificates Ze sends for this peer, and the most it accepts from it. RFC 7296 Section 3.6 requires an implementation be capable of being configured to send and accept up to four. The default is that figure, so an operator who never sets this leaf gets the conformant behavior. A peer that sends more than this is REFUSED, never truncated. A silent trim would pass a count check and hide from the operator that the limit was reached. It would also make which certificates survive depend on the order the peer chose.
        - **certificate-status-request** `boolean`: Check this peer's EAP-TLS certificate chain by the OCSP response it staples.
          RFC 9190 Section 5.4 recommends OCSP stapling for checking an EAP-TLS server's certificate chain, and puts a MUST on the peer that uses it: 'it MUST treat a CertificateEntry (but not the trust anchor) without a valid CertificateStatus extension as invalid and abort the handshake with an appropriate alert'. This leaf is what makes Ze such a peer. With it true, Ze refuses an authenticator that staples nothing, staples a response about another certificate, staples an expired one, or staples one that reports the certificate revoked or unknown. It also refuses a chain carrying an intermediate below the trust anchor, because Ze reads a stapled status for the leaf certificate alone and Section 5.4 makes an entry whose status it cannot read invalid. With it false, which is the default, Ze checks the same chain against the crl of the ca it validates against. Section 5.4 requires that check on TLS 1.3 either way. It governs the peer role. As the authenticator Ze answers a Certificate Status Request whenever the pki certificate it presents carries an ocsp-response, whatever this leaf says.
        - **certificate-url** `string`: The http URL at which this device publishes its own certificate.
          The http URL at which this device's own certificate is published, sent beside the SHA-1 hash when hash-and-url is true. RFC 7296 Section 3.6 requires support for the http scheme.
        - **certificate-url-allow** `ip-prefix[]`: Extra destinations a certificate URL from this peer CAN resolve to.
          Destinations a certificate URL received from this peer CAN resolve to, beyond the fetcher's defaults. The fetcher refuses loopback, private, link-local and multicast addresses, and the cloud metadata address. It refuses them because the daemon runs on a router and holds routes an internet host does not. Naming a prefix here permits it.
        - **hash-and-url** `boolean`: Use the Hash and URL certificate encodings of RFC 7296 Section 3.6.
          When it is true Ze sends its certificate as a SHA-1 hash plus certificate-url, advertises HTTP_CERT_LOOKUP_SUPPORTED, and resolves a peer's Hash and URL payload. It defaults to false, and that default is a security property. Resolving a peer's payload fetches a URL that peer chose, and Ze must do that before it CAN authenticate the peer. With this leaf false Ze advertises nothing, a conforming peer sends no such payload, a non-conforming one is dropped, and no fetch is reachable. The enabled fetch takes the http scheme only, a 64 KiB cap, a 5 second timeout, no redirects, denied destinations, and SHA-1 verification before any parser.
        - **local-id** `string`: Local identity for IKE negotiation.
          Ze derives the ID type it sends from the shape of the value. An IP address literal goes out as ID_IPV4_ADDR or ID_IPV6_ADDR, and every other value as ID_FQDN. There is no ID_DER_ASN1_DN form, so commit refuses a distinguished name. Commit also refuses a subtree or an address range, because this leaf names the one identity Ze asserts. An empty leaf sends the peer name.
        - **mode** `enumeration`: Authentication mode.
          eap-md5 establishes no shared key, and RFC 7296 Section 2.16 discourages such a method: EAP methods that do not establish a shared key SHOULD NOT be used, as they are subject to a number of man-in-the-middle attacks. The IKEv2 AUTH payloads are then keyed by SK_pi and SK_pr instead of by an EAP MSK. The method authenticates this peer to the far end and tells this peer nothing about the far end. The daemon writes one warning when this mode is adopted. Use eap-tls or eap-mschapv2 unless the far end runs no other method.
          - `eap-md5`: EAP MD5-Challenge, Type 4 (RFC 3748 Section 5.4).
